<div class="quickstart-hero">
<h1>FishSET GUI Quickstart Guide</h1>
<p>FishSET is a set of statistical programming and data management tools for organizing fishery data, creating model inputs, and evaluating policy scenarios. This guide gives new users a practical path through the FishSET GUI.</p>
<p><strong>Recommended path:</strong> Upload Data &rarr; Select variables &rarr; QAQC &rarr; Explore the data &rarr; Format Data &rarr; Modeling &rarr; Policy</p>
</div>

<div class="quickstart-grid">
<div class="quickstart-card"><h3>What the GUI does</h3><p>The GUI helps you move from raw data to model-ready outputs without writing code. It guides data loading, quality checks, derived variables, model fitting, and policy analysis.</p></div>
<div class="quickstart-card"><h3>Before you start</h3><ul><li>Have your main data file ready. Port, spatial, gridded, and auxiliary files are optional.</li><li>Choose a FishSET folder where project files can be saved.</li><li>For mapping or policy tabs, make sure your spatial data contain the required zone information.</li></ul></div>
<div class="quickstart-card"><h3>What gets saved</h3><ul><li>Project data and edits are stored in the local FishSET database.</li><li>Plots and tables are written to the project output folder.</li><li>Function calls and input values are written to the project logs.</li><li>The report template is stored in the project <code>doc</code> folder.</li></ul></div>
</div>

<div class="quickstart-note"><strong>Open the app:</strong> run <code>library(FishSET)</code> and then <code>run_fishset_gui()</code> in R or RStudio. The main data table is required; supporting files depend on your workflow.</div>

<h2>Quick path through the app</h2>

<div class="quickstart-path">
<details><summary>1. Information across all tabs</summary><p>Every tab includes controls to refresh or close the app, save plots and tables to the project <code>output</code> folder, record notes, and run an R expression.</p><p>Within the app, the primary data frame is <code>values$dataset</code>. Refreshing restores the original loaded table unless a different table is selected on <strong>Upload Data</strong>.</p></details>

<details><summary>2. Upload Data</summary><p>Set the FishSET folder, create or select a project, and load the files used in the analysis.</p><ul><li>The primary table is required; port, spatial, auxiliary, and gridded files are optional or workflow-specific.</li><li>Load files from a local location or from the FishSET database, then select <strong>Load data</strong>.</li><li>Use <strong>Manage Tables</strong>, <strong>Metadata</strong>, confidentiality settings, and <strong>Reset log</strong> to manage project files and records.</li></ul></details>

<details><summary>3. Select Variables</summary><p>Identify the columns that FishSET uses throughout the workflow.</p><ul><li>Assign IDs, dates, coordinates, catch, price, and zone variables.</li><li>Create haul, trip, seasonal, or zone identifiers when they are not already present.</li><li>Check the saved mapping before moving to data checks or model preparation.</li></ul></details>

<details><summary>4. Data Quality Evaluation</summary><p>Find and correct common issues before analysis, including missing values, empty variables, duplicate records, incorrect classes, outliers, and invalid coordinates.</p><ul><li>Review the check results and use the available correction controls.</li><li>Spatial checks can identify points on land, outside zones, on boundaries, or at sea.</li><li>Save revised data to the FishSET database; <strong>Refresh data</strong> discards unsaved changes.</li></ul></details>

<details><summary>5. Data Exploration</summary><p>View loaded data as tables or plots before modeling.</p><ul><li>Edit cells, remove redundant columns, filter records, and save the revised table.</li><li>Use temporal, spatial, and x-y plots to examine patterns and relationships.</li><li>Gridded data can be aggregated and plotted by location; detailed interactive maps are available in <strong>Map Viewer</strong>.</li></ul></details>

<details><summary>6. Fleet Analysis and Assignment</summary><p>Define fleets, assign vessels, and summarize data at the fleet level.</p><ul><li>Build or load a fleet definition table, then assign vessels using string or dummy variables.</li><li>Fleet summaries include vessel counts, catch, bycatch, effort, trip duration, and density plots.</li><li>Run the selected summary function and save its plots or tables to the project output folder.</li></ul></details>

<details><summary>7. Simple Analyses</summary><p>Explore correlations and simple linear regressions among selected variables.</p><ul><li>Select variables and review the correlation matrix or regression results.</li><li>Use the plots to assess relationships and potential transformations.</li><li>Both plot and table results can be downloaded.</li></ul></details>

<details><summary>8. Compute New Variables</summary><p>Derive variables such as CPUE, identifiers, time measures, spatial measures, and trip summaries.</p><ul><li>Functions are grouped into arithmetic, transformations, dummy variables, nominal IDs, temporal, spatial, and trip-level categories.</li><li>Run a function, review the new column, provide a name if needed, and save the revised data.</li><li>Spatial functions require an appropriate spatial file; trip-level functions can calculate distance, centroids, or collapse haul data.</li></ul></details>

<details><summary>9. Map Viewer</summary><p>Display the spatial distribution of hauls and related values on an interactive map.</p><ul><li>A spatial zone file and a zone identifier linking the primary data to the map are required.</li><li>Select numeric, temporal, ID, and point-or-path variables, then press <strong>Run</strong>.</li><li>Hover over map points for details and use the accompanying plots to explore patterns. The map itself cannot be saved.</li></ul></details>

<details><summary>10. Define Alternative Fishing Choices</summary><p>Define the alternative locations and distance matrix used by choice models.</p><ul><li>Choose whether starting and alternative locations come from zone centroids, ports, or longitude/latitude variables.</li><li>The distance matrix can be generated from haul-level or gridded data and returned in miles, kilometers, or meters.</li><li>Use the haul-count summary to exclude zones with insufficient observations.</li></ul></details>

<details><summary>11. Expected Catch/Revenue</summary><p>Calculate expected catch or revenue for alternative fishing zones. A catch variable is required; add price or value to calculate revenue.</p><ul><li>Choose fleet or grouped calculations and select the temporal sorting and averaging options.</li><li>The output includes standard short-, medium-, and long-term matrices used by the conditional logit model.</li><li>Review the sparsity table before filling missing values or choosing a broader time window.</li></ul></details>

<details><summary>12. Format Model Data</summary><p>Assemble the distance, expected catch or revenue, and other matrices into the structure required by the models.</p><p>Run this step after the supporting variables and matrices have been created, and verify the resulting model data before designing a model.</p></details>

<details><summary>13. Models</summary><p>Define, fit, and compare discrete choice models.</p><ul><li>Use <strong>Model Design</strong> to specify formulas, likelihoods, and other model parameters.</li><li>Use <strong>Model Fit</strong> to estimate and save model objects.</li><li>Use <strong>Model Cross Validation</strong> to assess out-of-sample performance and compare candidate models.</li></ul></details>

<details><summary>14. Policy</summary><p>Evaluate management scenarios and their effects on effort and welfare.</p><ul><li>Use <strong>Zone Closure</strong> to define closed or restricted areas.</li><li>Run <strong>Policy Simulations</strong> to estimate effort redistribution and welfare impacts.</li><li>Review the effort and welfare summary tabs after each scenario.</li></ul></details>

<details><summary>15. Bookmark Choices</summary><p>Save the current GUI selections so they can be restored later.</p><p>Reloading restores selections but does not reload data or rerun functions. Save the data first, then reload it after opening the bookmarked state.</p></details>
</div>
